scopeNote: Concise study notes to orient revision. They are not a substitute for institution-approved teaching, clinical supervision, or current Kenya Ministry of Health protocols. Treatment details are intentionally not prescribed here.

notes.title: Anatomical terminology, planes, tissues, and body systems
notes.text: Use standard directional terms (such as anterior/posterior, medial/lateral, and proximal/distal) relative to anatomical position. Planes describe sections of the body; tissues combine to form organs, and organs work together in systems.

notes.title: Upper limb
notes.text: Study bones and joints alongside muscle actions, nerve roots, peripheral nerve territories, and arterial supply. Link structure to examination findings such as weakness, sensory loss, deformity, and injury patterns.

notes.title: Lower limb
notes.text: Relate hip, knee, ankle, and foot anatomy to weight-bearing, gait, major muscle groups, dermatomes, peripheral nerves, and pulses. Practice a systematic neurovascular examination after injury.

notes.title: Thorax
notes.text: Organize the thorax into chest wall, pleural cavities, lungs, mediastinum, heart, and great vessels. Surface landmarks help localize examination findings and guide safe clinical assessment.

notes.title: Abdomen and pelvis
notes.text: Use abdominal regions and quadrants to describe pain and organize differential diagnoses. Learn peritoneal spaces, abdominal organs, pelvic structures, vessels, and clinically important referred pain patterns.

notes.title: Head, neck, and neuroanatomy
notes.text: Map cranial nerves to their functions and examination tests. Connect brain regions, spinal tracts, meninges, and vascular territories to motor, sensory, language, visual, and coordination findings.

notes.title: Embryology and developmental anatomy
notes.text: Study fertilization, germ layers, folding, organogenesis, and placental development as a timeline. Relate disrupted development to congenital anomalies while avoiding assumptions about cause from appearance alone.

notes.title: Cell physiology and homeostasis
notes.text: Homeostasis maintains internal conditions through sensors, control centres, and effectors, commonly using negative feedback. Membrane transport, receptors, and cell signalling explain how tissues respond to changing conditions.

notes.title: Blood and cardiovascular physiology
notes.text: Blood transports gases, nutrients, hormones, and immune components. Cardiac output depends on heart rate and stroke volume; pressure, resistance, and vessel compliance shape tissue perfusion.

notes.title: Respiratory physiology
notes.text: Ventilation moves air, diffusion exchanges gases across the alveolar-capillary membrane, and perfusion delivers blood for exchange. Oxygen and carbon dioxide transport depend on ventilation-perfusion matching and hemoglobin.

notes.title: Renal and fluid-electrolyte physiology
notes.text: The nephron filters plasma, reabsorbs needed substances, and secretes selected solutes. Kidneys regulate volume, electrolytes, acid-base balance, and contribute to blood pressure and red-cell production.

notes.title: Gastrointestinal and liver physiology
notes.text: Digestion combines motility, secretion, enzymatic breakdown, and absorption. The liver processes nutrients and medicines, produces important proteins and bile, and participates in metabolism and detoxification.

notes.title: Endocrine physiology
notes.text: Endocrine glands release hormones that act through specific receptors and feedback loops. Learn hormone source, target, stimulus, and effect to interpret disorders of glucose, growth, thyroid, adrenal, and reproductive function.

notes.title: Nervous system and special senses
notes.text: Neurons communicate through electrical signals and synapses. Sensory pathways detect stimuli, motor pathways produce movement, and special senses convert light, sound, taste, smell, and position into neural information.

notes.title: Reproductive physiology
notes.text: The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis regulates gamete production and sex hormones. Understand the menstrual cycle, ovulation, fertilization, pregnancy-related physiological changes, and lactation as coordinated processes.

notes.title: Biomolecules, enzymes, and metabolism
notes.text: Proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids have distinct structures and functions. Enzymes lower activation energy; their activity depends on conditions, substrate availability, and regulation.

notes.title: Carbohydrate, lipid, and protein metabolism
notes.text: Glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, glycogen metabolism, fatty-acid oxidation, and amino-acid pathways coordinate energy use and storage. Fed and fasting states shift the balance between synthesis and breakdown.

notes.title: Vitamins and minerals
notes.text: Micronutrients act as enzyme cofactors, structural components, antioxidants, or regulators. Deficiency and excess can affect multiple systems; interpret diet, absorption, clinical signs, and laboratory results together.

notes.title: Clinical chemistry and laboratory interpretation
notes.text: Interpret results using the patient's context, reference intervals, trends, and pre-analytical factors. Patterns across related tests are generally more informative than an isolated abnormal value.

notes.title: Nutrition and energy balance
notes.text: Energy balance reflects intake, absorption, storage, and expenditure. Assess dietary pattern, growth or weight trend, illness, social context, and specific nutrient risk rather than relying on a single measure.

notes.title: Bacteriology and antimicrobial principles
notes.text: Classify bacteria by structure, staining, growth, and virulence. Antimicrobial selection depends on likely organism, infection site, susceptibility, patient factors, and local stewardship guidance.

notes.title: Virology and mycology
notes.text: Viruses require host cells to replicate; fungi have distinct cell structures and may cause superficial or invasive disease. Diagnosis uses clinical context with appropriate antigen, molecular, microscopy, or culture tests.

notes.title: Immunology and infection prevention
notes.text: Innate immunity provides rapid barriers and responses; adaptive immunity uses specific B- and T-cell responses and memory. Infection prevention combines hand hygiene, standard precautions, vaccination, and transmission-based measures.

notes.title: Medical parasitology and helminths
notes.text: Parasites have life cycles involving hosts, tissues, and environmental stages. Exposure history, specimen choice, microscopy or antigen testing, and local epidemiology guide diagnosis.

notes.title: Malaria
notes.text: Malaria is transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes and involves liver and red-cell stages. Recognize danger signs, confirm infection with appropriate testing, and use current Kenya MOH guidance for management.

notes.title: Cell injury, inflammation, and repair
notes.text: Cell injury may be reversible or progress to cell death depending on cause and duration. Inflammation recruits immune cells and mediators; healing may restore tissue or produce fibrosis.

notes.title: Neoplasia
notes.text: Neoplasia involves abnormal, relatively autonomous cell growth. Benign and malignant tumours differ in invasion and metastatic potential; diagnosis integrates clinical features, imaging, and tissue pathology.

notes.title: Hematology and transfusion principles
notes.text: Blood disorders affect red cells, white cells, platelets, or coagulation. Transfusion decisions require indication, component choice, compatibility, consent, monitoring, and current local protocols.

notes.title: Systemic pathology
notes.text: For each organ system, connect cause and mechanism to structural change, symptoms, examination, and tests. Compare common patterns and identify features that require urgent escalation.

notes.title: Specimen handling and diagnostic pathology
notes.text: Correct patient identification, specimen type, collection technique, container, timing, and transport preserve diagnostic quality. Label at collection and follow local infection-control and laboratory procedures.

notes.title: Anemia
notes.text: Anemia is reduced hemoglobin relative to an appropriate reference for age, sex, and pregnancy. Interpret symptoms, red-cell indices, reticulocytes, blood film, and likely cause; detailed notes are available separately.

notes.title: Classification and causes of anemia
notes.text: Mean corpuscular volume groups anemia into microcytic, normocytic, and macrocytic patterns. Reticulocyte response helps distinguish reduced production from blood loss or increased destruction.

notes.title: Red-cell indices and blood-film interpretation
notes.text: Read hemoglobin, MCV, MCH, RDW, and reticulocyte count together. A blood film can show cell size, shape, inclusions, and maturation changes that narrow the differential diagnosis.

notes.title: Iron, folate, and vitamin B12 deficiency
notes.text: Iron supports heme synthesis; folate and B12 support DNA synthesis and red-cell maturation. B12 deficiency can cause neurological features, so investigate it when macrocytosis or neuropathy is present.

notes.title: Hemolysis and inherited blood disorders
notes.text: Hemolysis shortens red-cell survival and may cause jaundice, reticulocytosis, and biochemical evidence of cell breakdown. Inherited disorders need confirmation, counselling, and longitudinal specialist-informed care.

notes.title: Bleeding disorders and transfusion principles
notes.text: Bleeding may result from vessel, platelet, coagulation-factor, or medication problems. Assess severity and stability; transfusion thresholds and products must follow current local policy and clinical supervision.

notes.title: History taking and presenting complaints
notes.text: Clarify the patient's concern, onset, chronology, associated symptoms, relevant medical and medication history, family and social context, and ideas or concerns. Summarize the problem and check understanding.

notes.title: General examination and vital signs
notes.text: Assess appearance, consciousness, hydration, pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, edema, and distress. Measure and interpret vital signs using age-appropriate reference ranges and repeat unexpected results.

notes.title: Cardiovascular examination
notes.text: Combine inspection, pulse and blood-pressure assessment, precordial palpation, auscultation, and peripheral signs. Relate findings to hemodynamics and investigate symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnea, or syncope.

notes.title: Respiratory examination
notes.text: Assess respiratory effort and chest symmetry, then compare expansion, percussion, and breath sounds systematically. Interpret findings alongside oxygenation, vital signs, history, and imaging when indicated.

notes.title: Abdominal examination
notes.text: Inspect before palpation, percussion, and auscultation, adapting order to the clinical situation. Localize tenderness, assess organ enlargement and peritoneal signs, and escalate severe or unstable presentations.

notes.title: Neurological examination
notes.text: Use a structured assessment of mental state, cranial nerves, motor function, sensation, reflexes, coordination, and gait. Localize the lesion by matching findings to neuroanatomy.

notes.title: Musculoskeletal examination
notes.text: Compare sides and assess look, feel, movement, function, and relevant neurovascular status. Examine adjacent joints and document deformity, tenderness, range, and functional limitation.

notes.title: Paediatric and obstetric examination
notes.text: Adapt examination to age, development, pregnancy, privacy, consent, and comfort. Use appropriate charts and protocols, involve caregivers appropriately, and recognize maternal or child danger signs.

notes.title: Aseptic technique and patient safety
notes.text: Prevent avoidable harm through hand hygiene, risk checks, patient identification, equipment preparation, and aseptic technique appropriate to the procedure. Explain the procedure and obtain consent.

notes.title: Medication administration principles
notes.text: Confirm the patient, medicine, indication, dose, route, timing, allergies, and documentation against an authorized prescription and local policy. Monitor response and report suspected adverse effects.

notes.title: Wound care and basic dressings
notes.text: Assess wound cause, dimensions, tissue, exudate, surrounding skin, pain, and infection risk. Use clean or sterile technique according to wound and local policy, then document and arrange review.

notes.title: Venepuncture and specimen collection
notes.text: Verify identity and requested tests, explain the procedure, select an appropriate site, and use safe sharps practice. Label specimens immediately at the bedside and follow transport requirements.

notes.title: Basic life support and initial stabilization
notes.text: Recognize unresponsiveness and abnormal breathing, call for help, and begin age-appropriate basic life support using current certified training. Follow local emergency algorithms and available equipment.

notes.title: Documentation, observation, and handover
notes.text: Record findings promptly, objectively, and legibly with date, time, and author. Communicate changes using a structured handover and confirm the receiving clinician understands urgent actions.

notes.title: Patient-centred communication and counselling
notes.text: Use open questions, active listening, plain language, and teach-back. Explore the patient's priorities and agree on realistic next steps while respecting culture and individual preference.

notes.title: Consent, confidentiality, and capacity
notes.text: Consent requires understandable information, voluntariness, and decision-making capacity for the specific choice. Protect confidentiality while following lawful safeguarding and reporting duties.

notes.title: Professional conduct and clinical records
notes.text: Maintain boundaries, honesty, accountability, and respectful conduct. Records should be accurate, relevant, timely, and handled according to privacy and institutional rules.

notes.title: Safeguarding, dignity, and culturally respectful care
notes.text: Recognize possible abuse, neglect, coercion, or vulnerability and follow safeguarding procedures. Provide privacy, explain examinations, seek consent, and avoid discriminatory assumptions.

notes.title: Teamwork, referral, and interprofessional practice
notes.text: Share clear, relevant information with the care team and know the limits of your role. Refer promptly when needs exceed available competence, resources, or facility level.

notes.title: Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics
notes.text: Pharmacokinetics describes absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination; pharmacodynamics describes drug effects and dose-response. Age, pregnancy, organ function, and interactions alter response.

notes.title: Prescription writing and medication safety
notes.text: A prescription must be complete, legible, and consistent with the authorized formulary and local rules. Reconcile medicines, check allergies and interactions, and clarify uncertainty before administration.

notes.title: Antimicrobials and antimicrobial stewardship
notes.text: Use antimicrobials only when indicated, select according to likely pathogen and local susceptibility guidance, and review results and response. Preserve cultures where appropriate without delaying emergency care.

notes.title: Analgesics, anaesthetic agents, and emergency medicines
notes.text: Understand indications, mechanisms, contraindications, monitoring, and adverse effects for each medicine group. Emergency medicines require protocol-based preparation and supervision appropriate to role.

notes.title: Cardiovascular, respiratory, endocrine, and gastrointestinal medicines
notes.text: Organize medicines by therapeutic target and class. For each, learn indication, mechanism, important cautions, monitoring, interactions, and the local guideline that governs selection.

notes.title: Adverse drug reactions and pharmacovigilance
notes.text: Suspect an adverse drug reaction when timing and clinical pattern are plausible and consider alternatives. Stabilize serious reactions, document exposures, and report through the appropriate national and local system.

notes.title: Cardiology and cardiovascular medicine
notes.text: Organize presentations into chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, edema, and shock. Link history, pulse, blood pressure, ECG, and examination to a differential; urgent presentations need immediate escalation.

notes.title: Respiratory medicine
notes.text: Approach cough, breathlessness, wheeze, chest pain, and hemoptysis systematically. Combine exposure history, oxygenation, respiratory examination, and appropriate investigations; recognize respiratory distress early.

notes.title: Gastroenterology and hepatology
notes.text: Classify abdominal symptoms by location, timing, bowel change, bleeding, and systemic features. Interpret liver tests as patterns and consider hydration, nutrition, medication exposure, and urgent abdominal signs.

notes.title: Renal and urinary medicine
notes.text: Assess urine output, fluid status, blood pressure, urinalysis, renal function, and medication exposures. Distinguish acute change from chronic disease and identify electrolyte or volume-related instability.

notes.title: Neurology
notes.text: Localize neurological symptoms by onset, distribution, and examination findings. Sudden focal deficits, seizures, altered consciousness, or rapidly progressive weakness require urgent assessment.

notes.title: Endocrinology and diabetes
notes.text: Endocrine disorders arise from hormone excess, deficiency, resistance, or feedback disruption. Assess symptoms and relevant laboratory patterns; acute metabolic decompensation requires protocol-based urgent care.

notes.title: Infectious and tropical diseases
notes.text: Use exposure, geography, time course, examination, and diagnostic tests to frame infectious differentials. Apply infection prevention, notify where required, and use current national protocols for treatment.

notes.title: Hematology
notes.text: Interpret full blood count, indices, reticulocytes, smear, and coagulation results as patterns. Consider marrow production, destruction, loss, and malignancy, and escalate severe cytopenias or bleeding.

notes.title: Rheumatology and musculoskeletal medicine
notes.text: Differentiate inflammatory, degenerative, crystal, infectious, and traumatic patterns using time course, joint distribution, systemic features, and examination. A hot acutely painful joint needs urgent evaluation.

notes.title: Dermatology
notes.text: Describe lesions by primary morphology, distribution, color, border, and evolution. Include medication, exposure, and systemic history; mucosal involvement, blistering, or severe drug reactions need urgent review.

notes.title: Surgical principles, asepsis, and perioperative care
notes.text: Safe surgery includes assessment, informed consent, identity and site checks, infection prevention, appropriate monitoring, and clear postoperative plans. Escalate deterioration promptly.

notes.title: Acute abdomen and gastrointestinal surgery
notes.text: Assess stability first, then pain, vomiting, bowel function, examination, and relevant tests. Peritonism, shock, obstruction, or suspected perforation warrants urgent surgical assessment.

notes.title: Trauma, burns, and wound management
notes.text: Prioritize life-threatening injury using a structured trauma approach and reassess after interventions. Document mechanism, neurovascular status, wound or burn extent, and arrange urgent referral when indicated.

notes.title: Orthopaedics and fracture care
notes.text: Describe fracture mechanism, alignment, skin condition, and distal neurovascular findings before and after intervention. Immobilization and referral depend on injury, patient, and local protocols.

notes.title: Urology
notes.text: Assess urinary symptoms, retention, hematuria, pain, infection features, and renal impact. Acute retention, obstructed infected systems, severe bleeding, or testicular emergencies need urgent care.

notes.title: Neurosurgery principles
notes.text: Recognize neurological decline, head injury red flags, spinal cord compromise, and raised intracranial pressure features. Stabilize and arrange urgent referral; avoid delaying transfer for nonessential investigations.

notes.title: Breast and endocrine surgery
notes.text: Assess a breast or neck mass by history, examination, and appropriate imaging or tissue pathways. Document red flags and use established referral pathways rather than assuming benignity.

notes.title: Anaesthesia and pain management
notes.text: Safe anaesthesia requires pre-assessment, airway and risk planning, monitoring, consent, and recovery observation. Pain management should be individualized, multimodal where appropriate, and protocol-guided.

notes.title: Postoperative complications and referral
notes.text: Monitor for bleeding, infection, thromboembolism, respiratory compromise, ileus, and wound problems. Use trends and early warning signs to escalate before deterioration.

notes.title: Growth, development, and nutrition
notes.text: Plot serial measurements on appropriate growth charts and interpret trends, not single values. Assess developmental domains, feeding, caregiver concerns, and possible regression or safeguarding risks.

notes.title: Newborn assessment and neonatal emergencies
notes.text: Assess transition, temperature, feeding, breathing, tone, and danger signs. Newborn respiratory distress, poor feeding, temperature instability, or reduced responsiveness requires urgent protocol-based care.

notes.title: Common childhood infections
notes.text: Assess general danger signs, hydration, respiratory effort, fever duration, immunization, and exposure. Use age-appropriate national guidance and recognize sepsis or severe infection early.

notes.title: Respiratory, gastrointestinal, and neurological conditions
notes.text: Children can deteriorate quickly; assess work of breathing, hydration, consciousness, and age-specific vital signs. Match tests and escalation to severity and current paediatric protocols.

notes.title: Immunization and preventive child health
notes.text: Use the current Kenya immunization schedule and document doses accurately. Combine preventive visits with growth monitoring, nutrition, developmental surveillance, and caregiver counselling.

notes.title: Paediatric emergencies and safeguarding
notes.text: Stabilize airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, and temperature using age-appropriate protocols. Consider safeguarding when injuries or history are inconsistent and follow reporting procedures.

notes.title: Antenatal care and normal pregnancy
notes.text: Antenatal care monitors maternal wellbeing, fetal growth, risk factors, and prevention opportunities. Use current Kenya guidance for screening, supplementation, visit timing, and referral.

notes.title: Labour, delivery, and immediate newborn care
notes.text: Monitor maternal and fetal wellbeing and progress of labour using approved tools and local protocols. Maintain respectful care, infection prevention, preparedness, and timely escalation.

notes.title: Obstetric emergencies and complications
notes.text: Bleeding, hypertensive emergencies, sepsis, obstructed labour, and maternal collapse are time-critical. Call for help, stabilize, and follow current national emergency obstetric protocols.

notes.title: Postnatal care
notes.text: Assess maternal bleeding, infection, blood pressure, pain, mood, feeding, and newborn adaptation. Provide counselling and follow-up using current maternal and newborn guidance.

notes.title: Gynaecological disorders
notes.text: Assess bleeding, pelvic pain, discharge, masses, and reproductive goals with consent and privacy. Exclude pregnancy where relevant and identify acute bleeding, ectopic pregnancy, or sepsis risk.

notes.title: Family planning and contraception
notes.text: Offer balanced, non-coercive counselling on available methods, effectiveness, suitability, side effects, and return to fertility. Follow current national guidance and respect informed patient choice.

notes.title: Sexual and reproductive health counselling
notes.text: Provide confidential, nonjudgmental counselling about sexual health, infection prevention, testing, consent, and reproductive choices. Adapt communication to age, safety, and local law.

notes.title: Mental health assessment and mental-status examination
notes.text: Explore presenting concerns, function, history, substance use, supports, and safety. Mental-status examination covers appearance, behaviour, speech, mood, thought, perception, cognition, insight, and judgement.

notes.title: Common psychiatric disorders
notes.text: Assess symptom pattern, duration, distress, function, medical causes, and risk. Use recognized diagnostic frameworks and local referral pathways; avoid reducing a person to a diagnosis.

notes.title: Substance use disorders
notes.text: Ask sensitively about substance, amount, frequency, harms, withdrawal, and readiness for change. Assess overdose and withdrawal risk and link patients with appropriate medical and psychosocial support.

notes.title: Crisis care, suicide risk, and safeguarding
notes.text: Ask directly and compassionately about immediate safety, suicidal thoughts, plans, means, and protective supports. Do not leave an imminent-risk patient unsupported; follow emergency and safeguarding procedures.

notes.title: Psychotropic medicines and referral
notes.text: Know broad medication classes, intended effects, important adverse effects, and monitoring needs. Initiation and adjustment require appropriate competence, supervision, and current clinical guidance.

notes.title: Triage and initial assessment
notes.text: Prioritize by acuity, not arrival order, using the approved triage system. Identify immediate threats, obtain vital signs, begin stabilization, reassess, and document escalation.

notes.title: Airway, breathing, and circulation
notes.text: A structured ABC approach identifies and treats immediate threats in sequence while calling for help. Reassess after every intervention and use local emergency algorithms.

notes.title: Shock and resuscitation principles
notes.text: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion with multiple possible causes. Recognize altered mentation, poor perfusion, and abnormal vital signs; identify the cause and follow current resuscitation protocols.

notes.title: Altered consciousness and seizures
notes.text: Stabilize airway and breathing, check reversible causes such as glucose, and characterize onset and duration. Persistent seizure, new focal deficit, injury, pregnancy, or failure to recover needs urgent escalation.

notes.title: Poisoning and envenomation
notes.text: Ensure scene and staff safety, identify exposure and timing, assess ABCs, and contact toxicology or referral support. Avoid unverified remedies and follow current poison-management protocols.

notes.title: Trauma and mass-casualty principles
notes.text: Use structured trauma assessment, triage, and repeated reassessment. In mass-casualty incidents, follow incident command and local triage policy, prioritizing interventions with greatest immediate benefit.

notes.title: Emergency referral and stabilization
notes.text: Stabilize within available capability, communicate early with the receiving facility, and arrange safe transfer. Send observations, treatments, key results, and a concise handover with the patient.

notes.title: Common eye conditions and vision assessment
notes.text: Check visual acuity for each eye and document method and correction. Assess pain, redness, discharge, pupils, and visual change; sudden vision loss requires urgent specialist assessment.

notes.title: Red eye, ocular injury, and urgent referral
notes.text: Pain, photophobia, reduced vision, chemical exposure, penetrating injury, or abnormal pupil are red flags. Protect the eye and follow emergency referral guidance; avoid pressure on suspected open-globe injury.

notes.title: Ear, nose, and throat assessment
notes.text: Take symptom and hearing history, inspect relevant structures with appropriate equipment, and document findings. Airway compromise, severe bleeding, or sudden sensorineural hearing loss needs urgent review.

notes.title: Common ENT infections and emergencies
notes.text: Assess fever, pain, swallowing, voice, hearing, and airway. Stridor, drooling, severe neck swelling, mastoid signs, or toxic appearance requires urgent escalation.

notes.title: Oral examination and common dental conditions
notes.text: Inspect teeth, gums, mucosa, tongue, and jaw opening, noting pain, swelling, trauma, and hydration. Facial swelling, spreading infection, trismus, or airway symptoms warrants urgent dental or medical referral.

notes.title: Full blood count and blood-film basics
notes.text: Interpret hemoglobin, white cells, platelets, indices, and differential alongside symptoms and trends. Confirm unexpected results and use a blood film when morphology may clarify the pattern.

notes.title: Renal, liver, and electrolyte tests
notes.text: Interpret creatinine and electrolytes with hydration, medicines, and baseline; interpret liver enzymes, bilirubin, and synthetic function as a pattern. Severe abnormalities or symptoms need timely escalation.

notes.title: Microbiology specimens and culture principles
notes.text: Choose the right specimen and collect it aseptically before antimicrobials when feasible and safe. Correct labeling, transport, and clinical details improve interpretation of culture results.

notes.title: Urinalysis and point-of-care testing
notes.text: Point-of-care tests support but do not replace clinical assessment. Check sample quality, timing, device controls, and limitations; confirm results when required by local protocol.

notes.title: ECG interpretation foundations
notes.text: Read systematically: rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, and waveform changes, then compare with symptoms and prior ECGs. A normal tracing does not exclude serious disease; urgent findings require escalation.

notes.title: Imaging selection and interpretation principles
notes.text: Select imaging based on the clinical question, urgency, radiation or contrast considerations, and local availability. Correlate the report with examination and seek senior review for uncertainty.

notes.title: Primary health care and health promotion
notes.text: Primary health care integrates accessible first-contact care, prevention, community participation, and referral. Health promotion supports people and communities to improve control over health determinants.

notes.title: Epidemiology and disease surveillance
notes.text: Epidemiology describes health events by person, place, and time and tests determinants. Surveillance continuously collects and interprets data to detect trends and guide public-health action.

notes.title: Communicable disease prevention and control
notes.text: Control combines case detection, reporting, treatment or isolation when indicated, contact measures, vaccination, and community communication. Follow current national case definitions and notification rules.

notes.title: Environmental health, water, sanitation, and hygiene
notes.text: Safe water, sanitation, food safety, waste management, and hygiene reduce environmental exposure and infection. Assess household and community conditions and coordinate appropriate public-health action.

notes.title: Maternal, newborn, and child community health
notes.text: Community-based care connects families with antenatal, skilled birth, postnatal, immunization, nutrition, and early-childhood services. Recognize danger signs and support timely referral.

notes.title: Occupational health and community diagnosis
notes.text: Assess workplace hazards, exposure pathways, protective measures, and worker health. Community diagnosis combines local data and participation to identify priority needs and plan responses.

notes.title: Health education and outreach
notes.text: Set clear learning objectives, use accessible language and locally relevant examples, and invite questions. Evaluate understanding and participation rather than measuring success by information delivered alone.

notes.title: Nutritional assessment
notes.text: Assess dietary intake, anthropometry, clinical signs, illness, and social context. Use appropriate age-specific measures and growth references; interpret trends and avoid relying on appearance alone.

notes.title: Macronutrient and micronutrient deficiencies
notes.text: Deficiencies may affect growth, immunity, blood formation, bone, and neurological function. Consider diet, malabsorption, infection, and increased needs; confirm and manage according to current guidance.

notes.title: Infant and young-child feeding
notes.text: Support age-appropriate breastfeeding and complementary feeding using current national recommendations. Assess feeding technique, growth, illness, caregiver circumstances, and safe food preparation.

notes.title: Therapeutic nutrition and nutrition in disease
notes.text: Nutrition plans should reflect disease, swallowing, digestion, metabolic needs, and patient goals. Severe malnutrition and refeeding risk require trained, protocol-based assessment and monitoring.

notes.title: Community nutrition and food security
notes.text: Food security includes availability, access, utilization, and stability. Community nutrition responses combine assessment, education, social support, and referral to appropriate programmes.

subjects.title: Research Methods, Biostatistics, and Evidence-Based Practice

notes.title: Research questions and study designs
notes.text: Frame focused questions using population, exposure or intervention, comparison, and outcome. Choose a design suited to the question and consider bias, confounding, and feasibility.

notes.title: Sampling, data collection, and ethics
notes.text: Define the population, sampling approach, variables, and reliable data procedures. Research involving people requires prior ethical review, informed consent, privacy safeguards, and responsible data handling.

notes.title: Descriptive statistics and basic inference
notes.text: Use counts, proportions, and appropriate measures of centre and spread to describe data. Confidence intervals and tests quantify uncertainty but do not establish clinical importance or causation by themselves.

notes.title: Reading clinical studies and guidelines
notes.text: Assess question, methods, population, bias, results, applicability, and conflicts of interest. For guidelines, verify issuing body, date, scope, evidence basis, and local relevance.

notes.title: Quality improvement and research project
notes.text: Quality improvement uses measured data to test changes in a local process. Define a problem, baseline, aim, change, outcome measure, and ethical or governance requirements.

subjects.title: Health Systems, Leadership, and Health Informatics

notes.title: Kenya health-system structure and referral pathways
notes.text: Understand the current organization of national and county health services, facility levels, and referral links. Confirm the correct pathway using current Ministry of Health and county guidance.

notes.title: Health service management and leadership
notes.text: Effective leadership coordinates people, resources, communication, and accountability toward safe care. Use supervision, delegation within competence, team feedback, and transparent problem-solving.

notes.title: Health records, data quality, and reporting
notes.text: Accurate records support continuity, surveillance, planning, and accountability. Maintain completeness, consistency, timeliness, confidentiality, and compliance with approved reporting processes.

notes.title: Quality assurance and patient safety
notes.text: Patient safety identifies hazards, learns from incidents, and improves systems rather than assigning blame alone. Use audits, checklists, feedback, and measurable improvement cycles.

notes.title: Health law, policy, and resource stewardship
notes.text: Practice within current Kenyan law, professional scope, and institutional policy. Stewardship balances safe, equitable care with responsible use of medicines, equipment, time, and public resources.
